claims.text: High-temperature wear resistance of FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings is governed by formation of a stable surface oxide layer.
The surface oxide layer acts as a lubricant.
Lubrication by the oxide layer reduces the friction coefficient.
Lubrication by the oxide layer reduces the specific wear rate.
The tested material is a FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coating on a conventional metal substrate.
In-situ high-temperature tribometry with simultaneous microstructural characterization is the intervention relative to the baseline.
The applicable high-temperature wear regime extends from 500°C to 900°C.
FeNiCrCoCu coatings will exhibit improved wear resistance at high temperature relative to room-temperature behavior.
FeNiCrCoCu coatings will exhibit a reduced friction coefficient at high temperature relative to room-temperature behavior.
The proposed mechanism applies under normal loads from 10 N to 50 N.
Increasing temperature should be accompanied by decreases in friction coefficient and specific wear rate.
Suppressing oxide-layer formation while observing no decrease in friction coefficient or specific wear rate with increasing temperature would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: If the oxide layer is the proposed lubricant, suppressing it and then observing no reduction in friction or wear is consistent with the mechanism rather than a falsification. A stronger falsifier would be that oxide suppression does not worsen wear or friction relative to an otherwise matched oxide-forming control, or that oxide formation correlates with higher wear.
